title: 2024 Smart-Meter Electricity Consumption Report
executive_summary: Analysis of 1,428 smart-meter readings across 2024 shows total consumption of 1,207,700 kWh at a mean of 846 kWh per reading. Industrial sites dominate usage, accounting for over 82% of total energy. Consumption dipped mid-year before recovering strongly in Q4, and the second half of the year outpaced the first by 4.7%. Tariff split is near-even, and a moderate negative correlation between temperature and commercial energy use on hot days warrants further investigation.

key_findings.statement: Across 1,428 readings, total electricity consumption reached 1,207,700 kWh, yielding a mean of approximately 845.7 kWh per reading.
Industrial buildings consumed the most energy at 995,362 kWh (82.4% of total), followed by Commercial at 196,367 kWh (16.3%) and Residential at 15,971 kWh (1.3%).
Quarterly consumption peaked in Q4 at 352,882 kWh, followed by Q1 at 319,678 kWh. Mid-year quarters were lower: Q2 at 270,277 kWh and Q3 at 264,863 kWh, indicating a U-shaped seasonal pattern.
Second-half consumption (617,745 kWh) exceeded first-half consumption (589,955 kWh), representing an increase of 4.7% from H1 to H2.
On hot days (temperature ≥ 25 °C), 19 commercial readings were recorded with a mean consumption of 415.3 kWh per reading, suggesting elevated but moderate load under high-temperature conditions.

The median consumption was 406.8 kWh with a sample standard deviation of 913.4 kWh, indicating high variability. The mean recorded temperature was 11.6 °C, with 62 readings missing temperature data. Among commercial readings with valid temperatures, the Pearson correlation between temperature and energy was -0.64, suggesting that commercial sites use less electricity on warmer days.

Off-peak tariff consumption (608,076 kWh) marginally exceeded peak tariff consumption (599,624 kWh), with peak accounting for 49.7% of total energy. Across 12 distinct meters, the highest-consuming single meter recorded 252,241 kWh.

limitations: 62 readings have missing temperature data, which may bias temperature-based analyses including the hot-day commercial filter and the temperature-energy correlation.
The hot-day commercial subset contains only 19 readings, making the mean and any derived trends statistically fragile.
With only 12 distinct meters, meter-level conclusions may not generalise to a broader portfolio.
The dataset covers a single calendar year (2024); multi-year comparisons are not possible from this export alone.
Residential consumption is very low relative to other segments, which may reflect under-representation of residential meters rather than actual low usage.
conclusion: Industrial sites drive the vast majority of electricity consumption, and a clear U-shaped seasonal pattern—lower mid-year, higher at year-ends—warrants attention for capacity planning. The modest H2 increase of 4.7% and the near-even peak/off-peak split suggest stable tariff utilisation. The negative temperature-commercial energy correlation and the small hot-day sample size should be investigated further with richer data before drawing operational conclusions.
